Augmentum - Artic Carbon - Sermilik fjord plankton interaction network

Author

Nathan Hubot

Introduction

This page presents an exploratory interactive network showing inferred associations between planktonic prokaryotic and eukaryotic communities in Sermilik Fjord, southeast Greenland, sampled during the Augmentum / National Oceanography Centre (NOC) Arctic Carbon research cruise aboard the MY Akula.

The network was inferred from paired 16S and 18S metabarcoding datasets and aims to explore potential ecological coupling between bacterial and microbial eukaryotic taxa across the fjord system. The associations shown here do not necessarily represent direct biological interactions, but rather statistical co-occurrence patterns that may reflect shared environmental preferences, bloom dynamics, trophic relationships, or broader ecosystem structuring processes.

Only the Sermilik fjord subnetwork is shown here. To make the visualisation easier to explore, the network is filtered to retain the more connected taxa within the fjord-specific subgraph.

How to use the graph

You can interact with the network directly:

  • drag nodes to rearrange the layout;
  • zoom in and out using the mouse wheel or the navigation buttons;
  • click a node to highlight its nearest neighbours;
  • use the search box to find a specific taxon;
  • larger nodes represent taxa with more network connections;
  • colours distinguish prokaryotic and eukaryotic taxa.

Sermilik fjord network

Interpretation

The Sermilik fjord cross-domain network reveals a structured pattern of associations between planktonic prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Rather than forming two separate communities, the network shows extensive interconnection between bacterial and eukaryotic taxa, suggesting coordinated ecological dynamics within the fjord ecosystem.

Several highly connected bacterial taxa occupy central positions in the network, including members of the Candidatus Nitrosopumilus, OM27 clade, RS62 marine group, Octadecabacter, and Pelagibacillus groups. These taxa likely represent ecological hubs linking multiple eukaryotic lineages and may reflect organisms responding strongly to phytoplankton-derived organic matter, nutrient gradients, or bloom-associated environmental conditions.

Eukaryotic taxa are distributed throughout the network rather than forming isolated modules. Dinoflagellates such as Dinophysis, Pentapharsodinium, Torodinium, and Pseudocochattonella, together with several prasinophyte-associated taxa, appear connected to multiple bacterial groups. This pattern is consistent with tight coupling between microbial eukaryotes and heterotrophic or particle-associated bacteria in Arctic fjord systems.

The network also displays a moderately modular structure, with smaller clusters connected through central bacterial hubs. Such organisation may indicate local ecological niches embedded within a larger interconnected microbial community. The prominence of prokaryotic connector taxa suggests that bacteria may play an important integrative role within the Sermilik planktonic ecosystem, potentially mediating carbon processing and microbial succession during bloom events.

Importantly, the inferred links shown here represent statistical associations rather than confirmed biological interactions. The network should therefore be interpreted as a hypothesis-generating framework that highlights candidate ecological relationships for future investigation.
